description: ML engineer & final-year SE student; Applied AI Lab Coach, VinUniversity; SCI-published ML researcher. I mentor a 4-member grade-10 team (Hanoi) for Challenge: Identify Earth locations analogous to lunar south pole base sites. Approach: transparent multi-criteria similarity scoring on open NASA data (SRTM/Copernicus DEM, LOLA, MODIS LST) + sensitivity analysis + interactive public map.
summary:
We developed STEM Discovery Lab: Moon & Mars Analog Sites, a bilingual interactive web platform (with both a live satellite API and a 100% offline USB mode) featuring a 2D map, 3D globe, 25 km x 25 km 3D terrain blocks, and 6 analytical charts.

To address Challenge 9, the lab locks the five familiar NASA-named examples as comparison controls and guides users through a Guess -> Measure -> See the Breaks workflow across 13 new candidate sites—or any custom Earth coordinate measured live from AWS Terrarium DEM and NASA POWER—against 9 Moon South Pole (LRO LOLA/Diviner) and 8 Mars (MGS MOLA) targets. An interactive aridity gate (<= 250 mm/yr) exposes intuition traps, elevating Namib Escarpment (0.509) for the Moon and Qaidam Basin (0.762) for Mars.

This project is important because it empowers high school STEM students without GIS or coding skills to perform audited, reproducible analog screening while recognizing four unbreakable off-Earth limits—gravity, vacuum, radiation, and regolith dust—instead of misleading "% similarity" claims.
details:
STEM Discovery Lab: Moon & Mars Analog Sites is an interactive, open-data web laboratory built by a team of 10th-grade STEM students (with mentor guidance) for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Challenge 9). It helps students and researchers identify, measure, and critically evaluate Earth analog locations for Moon South Pole and Mars exploration using audited NASA/ESA satellite datasets.

  1. Step 1 — Guess: Users select a priority criterion (steep/rough terrain, hyper-aridity, or diurnal temperature swing), inspect 13 candidate Earth sites (L01–L13), and record a hypothesis before viewing scores. The 5 classic sites already named in the NASA brief (Atacama, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Icelandic Highlands, Death Valley, and Hawai‘i) are locked as gray comparison controls to prevent reusing known answers.
    • Live Satellite Measurement Anywhere on Earth: Users can search any place name or click anywhere on the 2D map to run a live 25 km × 25 km terrain and climate measurement via our backend API, complete with an interactive 24 × 24 3D terrain block (×1–×5 vertical exaggeration), a 3D orthographic globe, and 6 synchronized analytical charts (SYNC-1..6).
    • The Aridity Gate (≤ 250 mm/yr) “Aha!” Moment: Toggling the precipitation filter shows how a single physical constraint flips rankings: without filtering, monsoon-drenched Deccan Traps (2,053 mm/yr) ranks #1 on lunar terrain similarity (0.694), but enabling the aridity gate excludes 6 wet sites and elevates Namib Escarpment (80.6 mm/yr, 0.509) to #1 for the Moon, while Qaidam Basin (17.4 mm/yr, 0.762) leads for Mars.
  2. Step 3 — See the Breaks & Export Brief: Users examine 4 Unbreakable Physical Breaks (gravity 1/6 g & 0.38 g, ultra-high vacuum / 610 Pa CO₂, space radiation, and electrostatic glassy/iron-oxide regolith dust) alongside site-specific limitations, then export a printable 1-page A4 Summary Sheet (desk-based screening aid — not field-verified) containing their initial hypothesis and 4-fragment data provenance.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Demystifies Planetary Analog Research: Enables high school STEM students without GIS/QGIS or coding backgrounds to test hypotheses with real satellite measurements in under 3 minutes.
  • Builds Critical Scientific Thinking: Trains learners to question averages, inspect data skewness and weight sensitivity, verify sources in ≤ 2 taps (linking directly to 9 audited data tables and read-only Google Sheets), and understand where Earth analogs break down.
  • Accessible Anywhere: Features a bilingual Vietnamese/English interface, a responsive single-column mobile layout for 4G field use, a Student/Mentor mode switch, and a 100% offline file:// / USB static package (≤ 2.5 MB) for school labs with limited internet.

Tools, Languages, Software & Data Used

  • Frontend: Vanilla HTML5, CSS3 (responsive & print stylesheets, light/dark modes), modular ES6+ JavaScript (no framework/build step), Leaflet 1.9.4 (offline-patched), embedded Natural Earth 110m borders, HTML5 Canvas (3D globe & 3D terrain block), and inline SVG charts/markers.
  • Backend & Infrastructure: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn, HTTPX, NumPy, Pillow, Pydantic, SQLite (response caching and anonymous analysis history), containerized with Docker and deployed on Railway (paired with static web hosting).
  • Satellite & Open Data (1.79 GB preprocessed & audited): NASA POWER v2.10.0 (12-month 2023 climate, with Open-Meteo ERA5 failover), LRO LOLA (20 m) & Diviner PRP (including 5.76M polar triangles), MGS MOLA (16 ppd), Copernicus/USGS DEM via AWS Terrain Tiles (Terrarium PNG), Nominatim OpenStreetMap (geocoding), and ESA Open Science Catalog (366 catalog products).
  • Verification & Hardware: Automated Python data-audit and fault-injection test harnesses, Playwright, and headless Edge browser testing on standard student laptops and 4G smartphones.

How Our Project Is Creative

  • “Anti-Cliché” Benchmark Locking: Instead of letting users pick famous NASA examples, we lock the 5 textbook sites as baselines and push discovery toward 13 under-explored candidates or custom live coordinates.
  • Interactive Intuition Traps: Turns dry normalization math into a visual discovery—letting students watch rankings flip in real time when turning on the aridity gate or shifting weight sliders (e.g., Karakum 0.830 flipping Qaidam 0.828 on Mars under sensitive weights).
  • Honesty-First Scoring: Explicitly refuses to label any site “X% like the Moon,” pairing every score with near-tie warnings, rank-flip bisection thresholds, and physical deal-breakers.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Data Integrity & Skewness: Audited raw anomalies (such as -999, -32768, and pole anomalies), applied log1p transforms to skewed precipitation/roughness distributions, and compared Min-Max, Z-score, and Robust MAD normalization against outliers.
  • Physical Commensurability: Separated the official 3-axis Moon score (0.375 slope, 0.375 roughness, 0.25 aridity) from the reference 4-axis Diviner score because Earth diurnal °C (with atmosphere) vs. lunar Diviner K excursion (in vacuum) is only a proxy, whereas Mars (CO₂ atmosphere) uses all 4 axes.
  • Fixed Baseline Denominators: Locked normalization denominators across the 18 reference sites so measuring new live user coordinates never distorts baseline scores or rankings.
  • Usability, Provenance & AI Transparency: Replaced desktop-only hover tooltips with ≥ 44×44 px touch-friendly provenance modals, preserved offline usability, and included an explicit AI Usage Declaration confirming that all scientific measurements come strictly from audited NASA/ESA open data
